target.title: fix(browser): time out download saves
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Browser download waits used the configured timeout only until Playwright emitted the download event. After that event, the timer stayed active, but an already-started `download.saveAs(...)` could still finish later and publish the requested output path after the browser tool call had already timed out.

## Why This Change Was Made

The download capture now carries the deadline cancellation state into the save path and checks it immediately before the atomic output publication step. A slow or delayed Playwright save can still finish its temporary write, but it cannot publish the final output after the waiter has timed out or been cancelled.

## User Impact

Browser download tools now fail with the configured timeout when Playwright cannot finish saving in time, and timed-out downloads no longer create the requested output file later after the tool has already reported failure.

## Evidence

- Current head `78a30bd85a9543bc89cbd685483f2e00762b685f` passed `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/browser/src/browser/pw-tools-core.waits-next-download-saves-it.test.ts`: 1 test file passed; 12 tests passed and 3 skipped.
- Current head `78a30bd85a9543bc89cbd685483f2e00762b685f` passed `git diff --check HEAD^ HEAD`.
- Real Playwright Chromium proof on Node `v24.18.0` exercised the current `createDownloadCaptureForPage` implementation with a real browser download. The proof patched the real Playwright `Download.saveAs(...)` for that download so the save completed only after the configured deadline rejected the waiter, then verified neither the temporary output nor the requested final output remained:

```text
proof-head: 78a30bd85a9543bc89cbd685483f2e00762b685f
real-download-url: http://127.0.0.1:62968/download
patched-saveAs-temp-basename: .fs-safe-output-33d0b278-12da-4936-9c3a-51ff04636159-artifact.bin.part
observed-rejection: Timeout waiting for download
elapsed-ms: 124
saveAs-call-count: 1
temp-output-exists-after-late-save: false
final-output-exists-after-late-save: false
proof-result: PASS late Playwright download save did not publish after timeout
```

target.title: fix(discord): bound Activity shell requests
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Discord Activity shell fetches its token and widget metadata without a deadline. If the gateway stalls before headers or while streaming a JSON body, the embedded Activity can remain stuck on its opening state indefinitely.

## Why This Change Was Made

Route both shell API calls through one 15-second `AbortController` helper whose timer remains active through `response.json()`. Successful responses require a usable JSON body, aborted error bodies propagate to the existing Gateway offline state, and malformed non-2xx bodies retain the existing HTTP status mapping.

The regression tests execute the generated `DISCORD_ACTIVITY_SHELL_JS` itself. They cover a pre-header token stall and a post-header widget-body stall, and model active timers so an implementation that clears the deadline after headers cannot pass.

## User Impact

A stalled Discord Activity gateway request now resolves to the existing retryable Gateway offline UI after 15 seconds instead of leaving the widget indefinitely stuck or rendering an invalid iframe.

## Evidence

### Exact revision and CI

- Exact head: `659b835fbb63b7adf6a5950bcf9b65cadf7a51dd`.
- GitHub `openclaw/ci-gate`: passed on the exact head ([run 29491455379](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29491455379)).
- Fresh focused run on Node 22.22.0: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/activities/shell.timeout.test.ts extensions/discord/src/activities/http.test.ts` -> 2 files, 24 tests passed.
- Targeted `oxlint`, `oxfmt --check`, and `git diff --check`: passed.
- Mutation proof: clearing the body timer immediately after response headers makes the behavior harness fail with `timer is no longer active`.

### Real Chromium request-boundary proof

Chrome 149 loaded the exact generated HTML/JS from this revision. A real Node HTTP server then controlled the two failure modes while the production shell used the browser's real `fetch`, `AbortController`, JSON body reader, and DOM rendering path.

- **Before headers:** the token request arrived at `+25467 ms`; the browser closed the still-headerless socket at `+40467 ms` (exactly `15000 ms` later). The rendered state was `Gateway offline`, with zero iframes.
- **During the JSON body:** the widget response sent `200` headers plus an unfinished JSON prefix at `+25487 ms`; the browser closed the unfinished socket at `+40490 ms` (`15003 ms` later, `writableEnded=false`). The rendered state was `Gateway offline`, with zero iframes.
- **Recovery:** after each failure, reloading the same browser page against healthy token and widget responses rendered `Recovered widget` with one iframe in `64 ms` and `62 ms`, respectively. The iframe document loaded successfully and the browser console was clean.

The initial absolute timestamps include Chrome startup and first navigation; the deadline assertion is request/partial-body event to socket close.

### Proof boundary

The harness substitutes only the Discord SDK handshake (`ready`, `authorize`, and `authenticate`) so it can reach the Activity shell's outbound request boundary without a Discord account. The pinned `@discord/embedded-app-sdk@2.5.0` contract was checked: its documented sequence is `ready` -> `authorize` -> application token fetch -> `authenticate`, which is the boundary used here. The network timeout, streaming body abort, offline UI, and recovery path are not mocked.

This is real-browser diagnostic proof of the changed behavior, but it is not a Discord-hosted Activity recording. No live Discord Activity was deliberately stalled.

target.title: Bound diagnostic config file read with size cap
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readConfigExport` in the diagnostic support export path calls `fs.readFileSync(options.configPath, "utf8")` on the user's config file with no size limit. A corrupted or enormous config file can OOM the diagnostic export path, preventing support bundle generation.

## Why This Change Was Made

PR #101472 established the bounded-read pattern. The diagnostic export path reads the user's config file to include sanitized config in support bundles. Config files are user-controlled content and should not be trusted to have reasonable size. Using `readRegularFileSync` with an 8 MB cap (config files are typically <100 KB) prevents OOM from corrupted config files while maintaining diagnostic value.

## User Impact

No user-visible change under normal conditions. Config files under 8 MB export identically to before. An oversized config file results in a graceful config-shape-read-failure entry in the diagnostic report instead of crashing the export.

## Evidence

- Replaced `fs.readFileSync(options.configPath, "utf8")` with `readRegularFileSync({ filePath: options.configPath, maxBytes: DIAGNOSTIC_CONFIG_MAX_BYTES })` at `src/logging/diagnostic-support-export.ts:353-356`
- Added `DIAGNOSTIC_CONFIG_MAX_BYTES = 8 * 1024 * 1024` constant
- Added `readRegularFileSync` import from `../infra/regular-file.js`
- Existing error handling already catches and reports read failures gracefully

target.title: fix(scripts): preserve surrogate pairs when truncating LLM text in bench dump
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`scripts/repro/tool-surface-live-bench.ts` uses `String.prototype.slice(0, N)` at three sites to truncate LLM output text for benchmark trail/log output. `slice` operates on UTF-16 code units, so when a surrogate pair (emoji, CJK character) straddles the cut boundary at position 299-300 or 399-400, the result contains an unpaired high surrogate — invalid Unicode that downstream consumers may reject.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replace with `truncateUtf16Safe` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`, the same helper already used across the codebase for safe UTF-16 boundary truncation. Sibling UTF-16 PRs (#104054, #107664, #109561, #109498, #109839) all use the same helper. The 300- and 400-code-unit limits and all non-truncated output remain unchanged.

Collision check: searched open PRs for `tool-surface-live-bench`, `truncateUtf16Safe`, `bench dump`; no same-file or same-problem open PR was found.

## User Impact

Benchmark trail and result dump output no longer produces invalid Unicode. No production impact — this file is a `scripts/repro/` bench tool.

## Evidence

I ran the same throwaway TypeScript probe against the real imported `truncateUtf16Safe` helper with boundary-straddling `🐱` (U+1F431) input at the same lengths used by the bench script's three truncation sites (300 for ASSISTANT text, 400 for TOOLRESULT and finalText).

Before the fix, with the three production truncation lines restored to `.slice(0, N)`:

```
{"fix":"before (raw .slice)","ASSISTANT_text_unpaired":true,"TOOLRESULT_unpaired":true,"finalText_unpaired":true,"assist_length":300,"tool_length":400,"final_length":400}
```

After the fix:

```
{"fix":"after (truncateUtf16Safe)","ASSISTANT_text_unpaired":false,"TOOLRESULT_unpaired":false,"finalText_unpaired":false,"assist_length":299,"tool_length":399,"final_length":399}
```

Focused regression suite after rebasing onto current `upstream/main`:

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/tool-surface-live-bench.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  8 passed (8)
```

Targeted `oxfmt --check` and `git diff --check` passed. I did not run a live multi-provider LLM bench, but the probe exercises the exact same production import, boundary lengths, and format strings used by the bench script's three truncation sites and verifies no trailing high surrogates at any site.

target.title: fix(security): bound skill-file audit read (restore removed fs dependency)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`main` is broken: `src/security/audit-extra.async.ts` calls `fs.readFile(params.skillFilePath, ...)` at line ~196 but has no `fs` import, so typecheck fails (`Cannot find name 'fs'`) and blocks CI.

## Why This Change Was Made

The "bound file reads in audit" series (#101773, #101775) converted the plugin-manifest read to the safe `readRegularFile` helper and removed the now-unused `import fs from "node:fs/promises"` — but missed the SKILL.md read added by #109363, which still used `fs.readFile`. That left an orphaned reference and a broken build.

## User Impact

Restores a green build. Consistent with the series intent, the skill-file audit read is now bounded via `readRegularFile` (cap `256_000` bytes, matching the workspace loader's `DEFAULT_MAX_SKILL_FILE_BYTES`) instead of an unbounded `fs.readFile`, so an oversized attacker-controlled `SKILL.md` cannot force an unbounded read during the code-safety scan.

## Evidence

- Single-file change: adds `MAX_SKILL_AUDIT_FILE_BYTES = 256_000` and converts the one orphaned `fs.readFile` to `readRegularFile({...}).then(({buffer}) => buffer.toString("utf-8"))`, mirroring the existing manifest-read pattern at line ~114. No remaining `fs.method()` calls; no `fs` import needed.
- The file was green at ab99029 (had `import fs`); this restores correctness after the import was removed.

target.title: Bound plugin bundle command file reads with size cap
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadBundleCommandsFromRoot` calls `fs.readFileSync(filePath, "utf-8")` on user-installed plugin bundle command markdown files with no size limit. A corrupted, enormous, or malicious command file can OOM the process during plugin bundle load.

## Why This Change Was Made

PR #101472 established `readRegularFileSync` / `readRegularFile` from `@openclaw/fs-safe/advanced` as the standard bounded-read primitive. This applies the same pattern to plugin bundle command file reads — the most natural extension of the bounded-read initiative, since bundle commands are user-installed content that should not be trusted to have reasonable size.

## User Impact

No user-visible change under normal conditions. Plugin bundle command files under 1 MB load identically to before. Files exceeding 1 MB are silently skipped with an error log instead of crashing the load path with an OOM or hang.

## Evidence

- Replaced `fs.readFileSync(filePath, "utf-8")` with `readRegularFileSync({ filePath, maxBytes: BUNDLE_COMMAND_MAX_BYTES })` at `src/plugins/bundle-commands.ts:112-117`
- Added `BUNDLE_COMMAND_MAX_BYTES = 1 * 1024 * 1024` constant
- Added `readRegularFileSync` import from `../infra/regular-file.js`
- `RangeError` from oversized file is caught and the command file is skipped gracefully
- Pattern matches PR #101472 (`src/cron/store.ts`) and PR #101477 (`src/cron/store.ts` archive pruning)

target.title: fix(gateway): isolate wizard exits from shared process
target.body:
Closes #110545

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway RPC wizard sessions inherited two CLI-owned behaviors that do not belong to a shared host process:

- setup/channel runners could terminate the Gateway through `runtime.exit()`;
- remote callers could not state whether setup should install the daemon, so downstream clients had to rely on an implicit CLI default.

In the Windows Companion beta.2 path this surfaced as a lost Gateway connection during `run-wizard`, before the Companion could finish its own lifecycle and verification steps.

Downstream consumer: openclaw/openclaw-windows-node#999.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Gateway owns the RPC process and request boundary, so both fixes belong in the same owner seam:

- run setup and channel RPC wizards with `createNonExitingRuntime()`;
- treat only `ExitError(0)` as normal wizard completion;
- preserve non-zero exits as explicit session errors;
- add optional `installDaemon` to `WizardStartParamsSchema` and forward `true`, `false`, or omission unchanged;
- keep RPC safety defaults `skipUi: true` and `suppressGatewayTokenOutput: true` explicit.

This consolidates and replaces #109412 so the protocol contract and host-lifecycle fix are reviewed together rather than as overlapping edits to the same handler and tests.

## User Impact

target.title: fix(config): ignore inherited keys when restoring env refs
target.body:
## Summary

Use `Object.hasOwn(parsed, key)` when restoring environment references so inherited properties are not treated as authored configuration.

## What Problem This Solves

`restoreEnvVarRefs` accepts plain-object values whose prototype may be customized. Its object branch iterates own `incoming` entries, but the previous `key in parsed` check also admitted inherited `parsed` properties. An inherited environment-reference template could therefore replace an incoming own value even though that template was never authored on the parsed object.

## Root Cause

- `in` traverses the prototype chain.
- `Object.hasOwn` matches the authored-key semantics used by adjacent config helpers.
- `isPlainObject` intentionally accepts custom prototypes, so narrowing the membership check is the correct local owner-boundary fix.

## Why This Fix

- One canonical own-property check at the restoration decision.
- No parser normalization, compatibility shim, or broader `isPlainObject` contract change.
- Matches sibling config-path and merge-patch own-key handling.

## User Impact

Normal JSON and JSON5 config behavior is unchanged. Internal or custom callers that pass plain objects with custom prototypes no longer restore inherited environment-reference templates.

## Evidence

- The original submitted test also passed with the old implementation, so the maintainer fixup replaced it.
- The repaired regression creates a custom prototype carrying an inherited template.
- With `key in parsed`, the focused suite fails because the inherited template is restored.
- With `Object.hasOwn`, the incoming value is preserved.

## Tests and Validation

- Blacksmith Testbox baseline: 1 focused regression failure with the old membership check.
- Blacksmith Testbox fixed: `src/config/env-preserve.test.ts` passed, 72/72 tests.
- Targeted `oxfmt --check` passed.
- Maintainer autoreview passed with no findings.

Not required: internal hardening with no documented JSON or JSON5 behavior change.

target.title: fix(sqlite): normalize BLOB/TEXT type mismatches during STRICT migration
target.body:
Related to #110186

## What Problem This Solves

The STRICT migration introduced in v2026.7.2 crashes the gateway on startup when legacy non-STRICT SQLite tables contain BLOB values in TEXT columns (or TEXT values in BLOB columns). The `INSERT INTO strict SELECT * FROM legacy` statement rejects the type mismatch, aborts the entire migration transaction, and leaves the gateway in a crash-loop with no in-product recovery — users must manually edit their SQLite database to proceed.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `node:sqlite` driver writes `Buffer.from()` JavaScript values as SQLite BLOB type. In non-STRICT tables, these BLOB values silently coexist in TEXT columns. When PR #108663 (`30ae21fca7`) introduced STRICT migration, it used a bare `INSERT INTO strict SELECT col1, col2 FROM legacy` that passes values through without type normalization. STRICT tables enforce column types, so BLOB-in-TEXT (or TEXT-in-BLOB) rows abort the INSERT and roll back the entire transaction.

Non-STRICT SQLite also allows BLOB and TEXT values with the same byte content to coexist as separate rows under a TEXT PRIMARY KEY (they have different stored types, so the UNIQUE constraint sees them as distinct). After CAST, these would collide. The migration detects this collision and fails with an actionable error rather than silently discarding data, consistent with the project's fail-closed policy for ambiguous persisted-state decisions.

Note: the linked issue #110186 also describes rowid-model and stale-lease startup failures that this PR does not change; those symptoms need separate resolution.

## User Impact

- Users upgrading from v2026.7.1 to v2026.7.2 whose databases contain BLOB values in TEXT columns (e.g., `config_health_entries.last_known_good_json`) no longer crash-loop
- The STRICT migration normalizes BLOB→TEXT and TEXT→BLOB via `CAST`, preserving all row data instead of aborting
- If BLOB and TEXT primary key values would collide after CAST, the migration fails with a clear error message directing the user to `openclaw doctor --fix` or manual cleanup — no data is silently discarded
- `openclaw doctor --fix` and the normal startup migration path both benefit — same fix, same code path

## Evidence

**Real environment**: Linux, Node v24.18.0 (SQLite bundled), branch `fix/strict-blob-text-cast-110186`, SHA `457d9ce36e`

### Real v2026.7.1→current upgrade through repairOpenClawStateDatabaseSchema (current head)

Created a canonical state database, downgraded `config_health_entries` to non-STRICT (simulating v2026.7.1), inserted a BLOB-in-TEXT row via `Buffer.from('{"api_key":"sk-prod-redacted"}')`, then ran `repairOpenClawStateDatabaseSchema`:

```console
=== Pre-downgrade (STRICT) ===
  path=/home/user/.openclaw/agents/main/agent/openclaw-agent.json vtype=null
  path=/home/user/.openclaw/openclaw.json vtype=text

BLOB row: {"config_path":"/home/user/.openclaw/credentials/ai.json","vtype":"blob"}

=== Running repairOpenClawStateDatabaseSchema (doctor) ===
Result: {
  "changes": [
    "Migrated shared state session watch cursors → provenance column (0 ambient, 0 sentinels removed)",
    "Migrated shared state tables to SQLite STRICT typing (1)"
  ],
  "warnings": []
}

STRICT flag: {"strict":1}

Post-migration rows:
  path=/home/user/.openclaw/agents/main/agent/openclaw-agent.json type=null value=null
  path=/home/user/.openclaw/credentials/ai.json type=text value={"api_key":"sk-prod-redacted"}
  path=/home/user/.openclaw/openclaw.json type=text value={"defaultModel":"sonnet-4.6"}

current_head=457d9ce36e
```

The BLOB value `Buffer.from('{"api_key":"sk-prod-redacted"}')` was correctly normalized to TEXT. All three rows migrated successfully with correct types and values. The doctor path completed without warnings.

### Scenario Matrix

Source type | Canonical column type | CAST behavior | Result
---|---|---|---
BLOB (Buffer) in TEXT column | TEXT | `CAST(col AS TEXT)` | ✅ typeof=TEXT, value preserved as UTF-8 string
TEXT string in BLOB column | BLOB | `CAST(col AS BLOB)` | ✅ typeof=BLOB, bytes preserved
TEXT in TEXT column (normal) | TEXT | `CAST(col AS TEXT)` | ✅ Idempotent, no change
BLOB in BLOB column (normal) | BLOB | `CAST(col AS BLOB)` | ✅ Idempotent, no change
NULL in TEXT column | TEXT | `CAST(col AS TEXT)` | ✅ NULL unchanged
INTEGER in TEXT column | TEXT | No CAST needed | ✅ STRICT auto-coerces INTEGER→TEXT
Non-UTF-8 BLOB in TEXT column | TEXT | `CAST(col AS TEXT)` | ✅ Bytes preserved, typeof=TEXT (SQLite does not validate UTF-8)
BLOB PK collides with TEXT PK after CAST | TEXT | **Fail-safe error** | ✅ Migration rejected with actionable error; no data silently discarded
BLOB PK with no TEXT collision | TEXT | `CAST(pk AS TEXT)` | ✅ Row preserved, PK value converted to TEXT

### Test output (engine-level, 20 tests including 6 new)

```console
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/sqlite-strict.test.ts --run
 ✓ |infra| src/infra/sqlite-strict.test.ts (20 tests) 176ms
     ✓ normalizes BLOB values in TEXT columns during STRICT migration
     ✓ normalizes TEXT values in BLOB columns during STRICT migration
     ✓ normalizes mixed-type rows in TEXT columns without losing values
     ✓ rejects STRICT migration when BLOB and TEXT primary key rows collide after CAST
     ✓ preserves BLOB primary key rows when no TEXT collision exists
     ✓ normalizes non-UTF-8 BLOB bytes in TEXT columns during STRICT migration
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  20 passed (20)
```

### Test output (state-DB doctor upgrade fixture, 85 tests including 1 new)

```console
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/state/openclaw-state-db.test.ts --run
 ✓ |unit| src/state/openclaw-state-db.test.ts (85 tests)
     ✓ doctor migrates legacy BLOB values in TEXT columns to STRICT without losing rows
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  85 passed (85)
```

### Test output (agent-DB upgrade fixture, 45 tests including 1 new)

```console
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/state/openclaw-agent-db.test.ts --run
 ✓ |unit| src/state/openclaw-agent-db.test.ts (45 tests)
     ✓ migrates legacy BLOB values in TEXT columns to STRICT without losing agent state
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  45 passed (45)
```

### Codex Review Resolution (PR #110186, July 18)

Codex P1 requirement | Status | Implementation
---|---|---
Real v2026.7.1→current upgrade proof via doctor/gateway (current head) | ✅ Addressed | Full `repairOpenClawStateDatabaseSchema` run at SHA `457d9ce36e` with BLOB data shown above
BLOB-to-TEXT normalization collision coverage | ✅ Addressed | New test: `rejects STRICT migration when BLOB and TEXT primary key rows collide after CAST` — migration fails with actionable error, no data silently discarded
Non-text BLOB byte handling | ✅ Addressed | New test: `normalizes non-UTF-8 BLOB bytes in TEXT columns during STRICT migration` — bytes preserved, typeof=TEXT (SQLite does not validate UTF-8)
Fail-safe for ambiguous conversion | ✅ Addressed | PK collision detection uses `typeof(pk) = 'blob' AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 WHERE typeof(pk) = 'text' AND CAST = CAST)` — colliding BLOB rows cause a clear error directing user to `openclaw doctor --fix` or manual cleanup; non-colliding BLOB PK rows are preserved and CAST
Closing link scope | ✅ Addressed | Changed `Closes #110186` to `Related to #110186` because the issue also describes rowid-model and stale-lease failures that this PR does not change

## What Changed

**`src/infra/sqlite-strict.ts`** (+76/-6):

- Added `columnTypes: Map<string, string>` and `primaryKeyColumns: string[]` to `CanonicalStrictTable`
- `readCanonicalStrictTables` now collects column types and PK columns via `PRAGMA table_xinfo`
- Before the INSERT, for tables with TEXT primary key columns, the migration detects BLOB/TEXT PK collisions and fails with an actionable error rather than silently discarding data
- The INSERT statement now uses `CAST(col AS TEXT)` for TEXT columns and `CAST(col AS BLOB)` for BLOB columns; all other columns (INTEGER, REAL, rowid alias) are passed through unchanged

**`src/infra/sqlite-strict.test.ts`** (+134):

- `normalizes BLOB values in TEXT columns during STRICT migration` — Buffer-in-TEXT → typeof=TEXT, value preserved
- `normalizes TEXT values in BLOB columns during STRICT migration` — string-in-BLOB → typeof=BLOB
- `normalizes mixed-type rows in TEXT columns without losing values` — TEXT + BLOB + NULL in same column
- `rejects STRICT migration when BLOB and TEXT primary key rows collide after CAST` — BLOB PK 'key-a' + TEXT PK 'key-a' → migration fails with actionable error, no data discarded
- `preserves BLOB primary key rows when no TEXT collision exists` — BLOB-only PK row is CAST to TEXT and preserved
- `normalizes non-UTF-8 BLOB bytes in TEXT columns during STRICT migration` — bytes `0x80 0x81 0xFE 0xFF` preserved as TEXT, hex unchanged

**`src/state/openclaw-state-db.test.ts`** (+59):

- `doctor migrates legacy BLOB values in TEXT columns to STRICT without losing rows` — full `repairOpenClawStateDatabaseSchema` path with `config_health_entries` containing BLOB, TEXT, and NULL rows

**`src/state/openclaw-agent-db.test.ts`** (+47):

- `migrates legacy BLOB values in TEXT columns to STRICT without losing agent state` — agent DB v8→current upgrade with `auth_profile_state` containing BLOB and TEXT rows

## What Did NOT Change

- Canonical schema definitions (no `openclaw-state-schema.generated.ts` or `openclaw-agent-schema.generated.ts` changes)
- Rowid model detection and comparison (`readTableRowidModel`) — issue #110186 also describes rowid-model failures that are not addressed here
- AUTOINCREMENT high-water preservation (`restoreAutoincrementHighWater`)
- Index, trigger, and view preservation (`readPreservedSchemaObjects`)
- Foreign key enforcement and restoration
- Column name matching (`assertMatchingColumns`)
- Startup migration lease acquisition — issue #110186 also describes stale-lease failures that are not addressed here
- `repairOperatorApprovalSchema` (its `typeof()` BLOB filter is redundant but harmless — kept as-is)
- Any runtime path outside STRICT migration
- Any config, env, or CLI surface

## Best-fix Verdict

- **Best fix**: Yes, as a partial fix for the BLOB/TEXT type mismatch portion of #110186. The CAST normalization belongs in `migrateSqliteSchemaToStrictInTransaction` because it is the single code path that performs the STRICT INSERT. PK collision detection is co-located because the collision is a direct consequence of type normalization. The fail-safe policy (reject with actionable error instead of silently discarding data) follows the project's fail-closed principle for ambiguous persisted-state decisions.
- **Refactor needed**: No.
- **Alternative considered**: Pre-migration `UPDATE` (rejected — extra scan, separate path); `--force` flag (rejected — bypasses safety); silent PK deduplication (rejected — irreversible data deletion without user consent per Codex review); fail with guided recovery only (viable but defers crash-loop fix — current fail-safe error already provides the recovery path).

## AI Assistance 🤖

- **AI-assisted**: Yes
- **AI model**: glm-5.1
- **Human confirmed understanding of code changes**: Yes

target.title: fix(telegram): time out incomplete Mini App auth bodies
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Telegram Mini App auth endpoint (`/__openclaw_tg_miniapp/auth`) had no bounded body-read lifecycle. An unauthenticated client could send an incomplete body and hold request-processing resources open.

The first version of this PR bounded the read, but real socket proof exposed a protocol bug: `readRequestBodyWithLimit` destroyed the request before the route could flush its intended HTTP 408. The client saw a silent close with zero response bytes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The route now uses the shared request-body guard, which owns the required response-before-destroy ordering for size and timeout failures. During the guarded read it also predeclares `Connection: close`, so the wire response agrees with the socket lifecycle; complete requests restore their original keep-alive state.

The regression test now uses a real `node:http` server plus a raw TCP client. It deliberately leaves a declared request body incomplete and asserts all three externally observable guarantees:

- `HTTP/1.1 408 Request Timeout`
- `Connection: close` with `Request body timeout`
- the client socket actually closes

## User Impact

Unauthenticated slow-body requests against the Mini App auth route are bounded by the shared 5-second pre-auth timeout. Clients receive a usable 408 response, the connection is closed, and normal complete requests retain keep-alive behavior.

## Evidence

### Focused regression test — exact head `70ed5884bb7d9b39af0e447e719732e73c8a916c`

```text
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/telegram/src/miniapp/routes.test.ts

Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  7 passed (7)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 13.97s
```

The timeout case is a real HTTP/TCP test, not a mocked `ServerResponse` or synthetic `Readable` assertion.

### Live Gateway A/B socket proof

Proof setup was isolated and credential-free: loopback-only Gateway, temporary state, Control UI disabled, gateway auth disabled only inside the isolated proof instance, and no Telegram token. The production Gateway plugin loader reported the proof plugin as loaded; that plugin only registers `registerTelegramMiniAppRoutes` built from the stated PR head. The request declared `Content-Length: 64`, sent only a partial JSON prefix, and deliberately kept its write side open.

Before the response-ordering fix (`b684f7ffff60ac26add071d7e3c5edf46a2cdff4`):

```text
connected=true request=partial-post writeSideOpen=true
elapsedMs=5043 end=true close=true error=none

<no response bytes>
rawResponseEnd
```

After the fix (`70ed5884bb7d9b39af0e447e719732e73c8a916c`):

```http

elapsedMs=5041 end=true close=true error=none
rawResponseBegin
HTTP/1.1 408 Request Timeout
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Connection: close
Content-Length: 20

Request body timeout
rawResponseEnd
```

Immediate post-timeout liveness probe against the same Gateway process:

```text

listener=127.0.0.1
```

This proves the incomplete client no longer remains open, receives the bounded 408 response, and does not destabilize the Gateway.

target.title: fix(discord): bound Activity shell requests
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Discord Activity shell fetches its token and widget metadata without a deadline. If the gateway stalls before headers or while streaming a JSON body, the embedded Activity can remain stuck on its opening state indefinitely.

## Why This Change Was Made

Route both shell API calls through one 15-second `AbortController` helper whose timer remains active through `response.json()`. Successful responses require a usable JSON body, aborted error bodies propagate to the existing Gateway offline state, and malformed non-2xx bodies retain the existing HTTP status mapping.

The regression tests execute the generated `DISCORD_ACTIVITY_SHELL_JS` itself. They cover a pre-header token stall and a post-header widget-body stall, and model active timers so an implementation that clears the deadline after headers cannot pass.

## User Impact

A stalled Discord Activity gateway request now resolves to the existing retryable Gateway offline UI after 15 seconds instead of leaving the widget indefinitely stuck or rendering an invalid iframe.

## Evidence

### Exact revision and CI

- Exact head: `659b835fbb63b7adf6a5950bcf9b65cadf7a51dd`.
- GitHub `openclaw/ci-gate`: passed on the exact head ([run 29491455379](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29491455379)).
- Fresh focused run on Node 22.22.0: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/activities/shell.timeout.test.ts extensions/discord/src/activities/http.test.ts` -> 2 files, 24 tests passed.
- Targeted `oxlint`, `oxfmt --check`, and `git diff --check`: passed.
- Mutation proof: clearing the body timer immediately after response headers makes the behavior harness fail with `timer is no longer active`.

### Real Chromium request-boundary proof

Chrome 149 loaded the exact generated HTML/JS from this revision. A real Node HTTP server then controlled the two failure modes while the production shell used the browser's real `fetch`, `AbortController`, JSON body reader, and DOM rendering path.

- **Before headers:** the token request arrived at `+25467 ms`; the browser closed the still-headerless socket at `+40467 ms` (exactly `15000 ms` later). The rendered state was `Gateway offline`, with zero iframes.
- **During the JSON body:** the widget response sent `200` headers plus an unfinished JSON prefix at `+25487 ms`; the browser closed the unfinished socket at `+40490 ms` (`15003 ms` later, `writableEnded=false`). The rendered state was `Gateway offline`, with zero iframes.
- **Recovery:** after each failure, reloading the same browser page against healthy token and widget responses rendered `Recovered widget` with one iframe in `64 ms` and `62 ms`, respectively. The iframe document loaded successfully and the browser console was clean.

The initial absolute timestamps include Chrome startup and first navigation; the deadline assertion is request/partial-body event to socket close.

### Proof boundary

The harness substitutes only the Discord SDK handshake (`ready`, `authorize`, and `authenticate`) so it can reach the Activity shell's outbound request boundary without a Discord account. The pinned `@discord/embedded-app-sdk@2.5.0` contract was checked: its documented sequence is `ready` -> `authorize` -> application token fetch -> `authenticate`, which is the boundary used here. The network timeout, streaming body abort, offline UI, and recovery path are not mocked.

This is real-browser diagnostic proof of the changed behavior, but it is not a Discord-hosted Activity recording. No live Discord Activity was deliberately stalled.

target.title: fix(shared): reject HTTP status codes outside the 100-599 range
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`extractHttpStatusMatch` in `src/shared/assistant-error-format.ts` only checked `Number.isFinite(code)`, so 3-digit sequences such as `"000"`, `"099"`, `"600"`, and `"999"` were accepted as valid HTTP statuses. Downstream code then:

1. Surfaced them as `"HTTP 0"` or `"HTTP 999"` in user-visible messages via `formatRawAssistantErrorForUi`.
2. Fed them into retry/classification branches (e.g. `isCloudflareOrHtmlErrorPage` checks `code < 500` and `code < 600`, so `code: 0` would pass both predicates and skip the Cloudflare code list).

The regex `\\d{3}` accepts any 3-digit number, but only 100-599 are valid HTTP status codes per RFC 9110.

## Fix

Add range validation `code >= 100 && code <= 599` to `extractHttpStatusMatch`. Both `extractLeadingHttpStatus` and `extractProviderWrappedHttpStatus` benefit since they share this helper.

```diff
 function extractHttpStatusMatch(
   match: RegExpMatchArray | null,
 ): { code: number; rest: string } | null {
     return null;
   }
   const code = Number(match[1]);
     return null;
   }
   return { code, rest: (match[2] ?? "").trim() };
 }
```

## Evidence

New test file `src/shared/assistant-error-format.test.ts` covers both helpers:

```
src/shared/assistant-error-format.test.ts
  extractLeadingHttpStatus
    ✓ accepts status codes in the valid HTTP range 100-599
    ✓ rejects 3-digit sequences outside the HTTP status code range
    ✓ rejects strings that do not start with a 3-digit HTTP status
  extractProviderWrappedHttpStatus
    ✓ accepts provider-wrapped statuses inside the valid HTTP range
    ✓ rejects provider-wrapped statuses outside the valid HTTP range

Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  5 passed (5)
```

Regression check on `extensions/ollama/src/stream-runtime.test.ts` (which uses `extractLeadingHttpStatus` for failover/retry logic):

```
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  105 passed (105)
Duration  50.45s
```

All existing tests pass, confirming valid HTTP statuses (503, 429, 500, etc.) are still correctly extracted.

target.title: fix(agents): report agent-delete cleanup failures instead of silent success
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw agents delete <id>` reported `ok:true` (and printed the removed directory paths) even when it could not actually remove the agent's on-disk state — when the Trash move failed, the agent's `agents/<id>/agent/` state and its `workspace-<id>/` directory were silently left behind. In headless/server environments where Trash is unavailable this happened on every delete: the operator saw success while orphaned state accumulated. A deleted agent id was also left dangling in `agents.defaults.subagents.allowAgents`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Found by the R5 QA campaign (skills/MCP/multi-agent lane, live repro). The delete path used a best-effort trash move that swallowed all failures and returned unconditional success.

## User Impact

`agents delete` now reports honest per-path cleanup outcomes: the response carries `removed: [{path, method}]` and `failed: [{path, reason}]`. The agent is still removed from config (exit 0 — the config mutation is authoritative), but text mode prints a warning for any path that could not be moved to Trash (with the path + reason so the operator can clean it up), and JSON exposes the outcomes. Deleted agent ids are pruned from default and per-agent `subagents.allowAgents`. No behavior change when Trash works.

Design note: this deliberately does NOT hard-delete on Trash failure. An earlier iteration added an `fs.rm` fallback; review surfaced multiple ways an irreversible recursive delete could hit unintended data (user-configured agent dirs, cross-agent overlapping workspaces, retained orphans, create/delete races). Since the reported bug is "stop lying about success," honest reporting is the correct, safe fix — no user data is ever deleted that Trash didn't already move.

## Evidence

- Protocol schema extended with `removed`/`failed` (`packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/agents-models-skills.ts`); CLI handles new + older gateway responses via optional fields.
- Tests cover trash-success (reports removed), trash-failure (reports `failed`, directory left in place, no deletion attempted), source-missing (lstat pre-check → `method:"missing"`), and allowAgents pruning.
- Autoreview (codex gpt-5.6-sol, xhigh): clean — "patch is correct (0.9)". Small, boring diff (agents.ts +47/−18).

target.title: fix(scripts): preserve surrogate pairs when truncating LLM text in bench dump
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`scripts/repro/tool-surface-live-bench.ts` uses `String.prototype.slice(0, N)` at three sites to truncate LLM output text for benchmark trail/log output. `slice` operates on UTF-16 code units, so when a surrogate pair (emoji, CJK character) straddles the cut boundary at position 299-300 or 399-400, the result contains an unpaired high surrogate — invalid Unicode that downstream consumers may reject.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replace with `truncateUtf16Safe` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`, the same helper already used across the codebase for safe UTF-16 boundary truncation. Sibling UTF-16 PRs (#104054, #107664, #109561, #109498, #109839) all use the same helper. The 300- and 400-code-unit limits and all non-truncated output remain unchanged.

Collision check: searched open PRs for `tool-surface-live-bench`, `truncateUtf16Safe`, `bench dump`; no same-file or same-problem open PR was found.

## User Impact

Benchmark trail and result dump output no longer produces invalid Unicode. No production impact — this file is a `scripts/repro/` bench tool.

## Evidence

I ran the same throwaway TypeScript probe against the real imported `truncateUtf16Safe` helper with boundary-straddling `🐱` (U+1F431) input at the same lengths used by the bench script's three truncation sites (300 for ASSISTANT text, 400 for TOOLRESULT and finalText).

Before the fix, with the three production truncation lines restored to `.slice(0, N)`:

```
{"fix":"before (raw .slice)","ASSISTANT_text_unpaired":true,"TOOLRESULT_unpaired":true,"finalText_unpaired":true,"assist_length":300,"tool_length":400,"final_length":400}
```

After the fix:

```
{"fix":"after (truncateUtf16Safe)","ASSISTANT_text_unpaired":false,"TOOLRESULT_unpaired":false,"finalText_unpaired":false,"assist_length":299,"tool_length":399,"final_length":399}
```

Focused regression suite after rebasing onto current `upstream/main`:

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/tool-surface-live-bench.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  8 passed (8)
```

Targeted `oxfmt --check` and `git diff --check` passed. I did not run a live multi-provider LLM bench, but the probe exercises the exact same production import, boundary lengths, and format strings used by the bench script's three truncation sites and verifies no trailing high surrogates at any site.

target.title: feat(kimi): show code quota in usage status
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Kimi Coding subscription users currently do not see code quota usage in OpenClaw status surfaces. This PR adds Kimi quota reporting to the existing provider usage/status pipeline so `5h` and `7d` windows can be shown instead of omitting Kimi.

This refreshed version also narrows the behavior for compatibility: automatic quota polling now only runs for the official managed Kimi Coding endpoint, and custom proxy/mirror base URLs are skipped by default.

## Why This Change Was Made

The quota payload is provider-specific (`GET https://api.kimi.com/coding/v1/usages`), so the Kimi provider plugin should own:

- auth resolution for existing Kimi credentials
- managed-endpoint gating for compatibility
- HTTP request + payload normalization

Core still only owns provider-id routing, usage aggregation, timeout handling, and status display.

This follows the existing provider-owned usage pattern already used by other providers, while keeping the Kimi implementation narrower in two ways:

- it reuses the existing Kimi auth sources (`KIMI_API_KEY`, `KIMICODE_API_KEY`, config/store resolution) instead of adding a new credential precedence path
- it does **not** assume that arbitrary custom proxies implement Kimi's managed `/usages` contract

The endpoint contract is not speculative: Kimi Code's official implementation also uses the managed usage endpoint in `managed-usage.ts`:

- https://github.com/MoonshotAI/kimi-code/blob/main/packages/oauth/src/managed-usage.ts

## User Impact

When OpenClaw has an existing Kimi Coding API key and the configured Kimi base URL resolves to the official managed endpoint (`https://api.kimi.com/coding[/v1]`), OpenClaw status surfaces can show:

- `5h` from the matching five-hour quota window
- `7d` from the top-level usage row

When users configure a custom proxy or mirror base URL for Kimi, OpenClaw now skips automatic quota polling instead of sending a best-effort `/usages` request to an endpoint whose response shape is unknown.

This PR does not change model request routing, model IDs, or auth precedence for normal Kimi model calls.

## Evidence

target.title: fix: surface stalled-session interruptions
target.body:
Closes #103905

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a stuck-session recovery could remove a channel's streamed draft without sending a terminal notice. A non-cooperative tool could also keep running after the owning turn was aborted, leaving the caller blocked until it eventually settled.

## Why This Change Was Made

The reply-operation terminal state now preserves `run_stalled` as a user-visible interruption while explicit user and restart cancellations keep their existing behavior. Tool execution races the existing cooperative `AbortSignal`, so an aborted run stops waiting while late tool settlement remains observed. Risk note: external side effects cannot be undone; the tool still receives the abort signal and its late promise is deliberately drained rather than delivered into the terminated run.

## User Impact

Users whose stalled turn is recovered now receive a clear interruption message instead of losing all visible trace of the turn. Plugin tools that honor cancellation can stop promptly, and tools that do not no longer hold the aborted turn open.

## Evidence

Focused regression proof drives the real reply-run registry expiry path into the production runner: `expireStaleReplyOperation()` records `run_stalled` and aborts the same operation before both terminal projections run. The tool abort proof exercises `wrapToolWithAbortSignal` with a non-cooperative handler. Negative control used the real pre-fix sources via `git show HEAD^ -- <files>`. 

Before (pre-fix abort wrapper): caller stays blocked after run abort while the non-cooperative tool keeps running.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a chat message with a managed outgoing image preview could remain pending indefinitely if the gateway `assistant-media` endpoint stopped responding. The `lit/until` directive would keep the placeholder forever while the underlying `fetch` stayed unresolved.

## Why This Change Was Made

`resolveManagedOutgoingImageBlobUrl` now attaches a 30-second `AbortController` signal to its `fetch` call. The deadline covers the response headers and the blob body read, and the timeout timer is cleared on every exit path. A `TimeoutError` is treated the same as an HTTP miss (returns `null`) so the UI falls back gracefully; non-timeout errors still propagate to preserve existing behavior.

## User Impact

Chat image previews now fail bounded instead of leaving a message row stuck on a spinner/placeholder when the gateway media endpoint hangs.

target.title: fix(ai): use fatal TextDecoder to reject malformed UTF-8 in ChatGPT stream responses
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Five `new TextDecoder()` instances in the ChatGPT Responses stream handler use the default non-fatal mode, which silently replaces malformed UTF-8 bytes with U+FFFD replacement characters. Malformed data from the API response or network is absorbed without detection.

Fixes the same pattern as #110502 (memory batch output).

## Fix

Switch all five `new TextDecoder()` to `new TextDecoder("utf-8", { fatal: true })`. Malformed bytes now throw `TypeError`, which is caught by the existing try/catch blocks in the stream processing pipeline.

All five call sites decode network data from OpenAI API responses where malformed UTF-8 can occur.

## Evidence

```
new TextDecoder().decode(malformed);
→ "�("  (silent U+FFFD replacement, data lost)
```

target.title: fix(config): restore process.env after invalid config rejection
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Config validation failures permanently pollute `process.env` with values from rejected configs.

When `loadConfigLocal` or `readConfigFileSnapshotInternal` loads `openclaw.json`, it writes `env.vars` entries to `process.env` **before** validation runs. If validation then fails (e.g. invalid `gateway.port`), the rejected config's env vars remain in `process.env` — the code never calls `restoreEnvChangesIfUnchanged` to clean them up.

In long-running gateway processes, this means:
1. User edits config, introduces an invalid value + a sensitive `env.vars` entry
2. Config watcher triggers reload → validation fails → error logged, but the sensitive env var is now in `process.env`
3. User fixes the config → reload succeeds → but `applyConfigEnvVars` never **deletes** keys absent from the current config, so the leaked value persists until restart

## Why This Change Was Made

The `restoreEnvChangesIfUnchanged` helper already exists and is correctly called for suspicious-config recovery and write-rollback paths. This PR adds the missing calls at every unsuccessful-exit boundary after env application:

- **Sync `loadConfigLocal` validation failure**: restore env before `observeLoadConfigSnapshot` so config health/audit observation never sees rejected env values, then throw
- **Sync `loadConfigLocal` duplicate-agent-dir rejection**: restore env after `findDuplicateAgentDirs` throws, matching the existing catch-log-rethrow pattern at `:1908`
- **Async `readConfigFileSnapshotInternal` validation failure**: restore env before `finalizeReadConfigSnapshotInternalResult` (already present from original PR)

The existing pattern at suspicious-config recovery (`:1872`, `:2140`) and write rollback (`:3079`) proves this is the correct primitive and ordering.

## User Impact

- **Before**: Invalid config → `process.env` permanently tainted with rejected values; env-derived observer storage paths (state dir, audit log) could be influenced by rejected config
- **After**: Invalid config → env vars restored to pre-load state before any observation, return, or throw
- No behavioral change for valid configs or already-working recovery/rollback paths

## Evidence

### Tests

- `pnpm test src/config/io.restore-env.test.ts` — **11 tests PASS** (5 unit + 6 entry-point regression)
- Entry-point coverage: sync loadConfig (schema failure + duplicate dir + changed value), async readConfigFileSnapshot (schema failure + changed value), valid config preservation
- `pnpm test src/config/io.observe-recovery.test.ts src/config/io.invalid-config.test.ts` — **43 tests PASS** (no regressions)

### Real Behavior Proof

Live proof script exercising `createConfigIO` entry points with real config files on tmpfs:

```

--- Proof 1: Sync validation failure ---
Config: {"env":{"vars":{"PROOF_SYNC":"should-not-survive"}},"gateway":{"port":"not-a-number"}}
Before: 'PROOF_SYNC' in env => false
Error (expected): Invalid config at /tmp/openclaw-proof-XXXX/.openclaw/openclaw.json...
After:  'PROOF_SYNC' in env => false
=> PASS - env restored

--- Proof 2: Sync duplicate-agent-dir rejection ---

After:  'PROOF_DUP' in env => false
```

target.title: fix(sandbox): make stat output locale independent
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #106576.

Sandbox `stat` previously treated missing files by searching `stderr` for the English text `No such file or directory`. That made normal `stat()` calls throw instead of returning `null` when the sandbox shell localized native error output.

## Why This Change Was Made

This moves the `stat` contract away from localized shell text:

- the anchored sandbox stat script now emits a fixed `__OPENCLAW_STAT_MISSING__` sentinel before invoking `stat` when the basename is absent
- successful stat output now uses GNU stat raw mode bits (`%f`) plus numeric size/mtime fields instead of localized `%F` file-type names and `%y` date text
- the remote fs bridge now parses the same raw mode bits for stat and hardlink checks, keeping the sibling shell-backed path aligned

Non-missing stat failures still throw, so permission/tool/runtime errors do not get collapsed into a false missing-file result.

## User Impact

Localized sandbox/container environments can now call sandbox `stat()` on absent paths without crashing the file bridge. File, directory, size, mtime, and hardlink behavior stays deterministic without depending on the host shell language.

## Evidence

- `git diff --check`

target.title: fix(codex): stop stale MCP child processes with revalidated SIGKILL escalation
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`killStaleComputerUseMcpChildren` in `extensions/codex/src/app-server/computer-use.ts:1146` sends `process.kill(pid, "SIGTERM")` and immediately records the pid as killed — without verifying the process actually terminated. If a child process traps or ignores SIGTERM (e.g. `process.on('SIGTERM', ...)` without `process.exit()`), it survives and becomes a zombie that the periodic health monitor can never clear.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix schedules a SIGKILL after a 2-second grace period. Before sending SIGKILL, it **revalidates process identity** using three checks:
1. **PID existence**: `process.kill(pid, 0)` — quick liveness probe
2. **Immutable launch identity**: `lstart` (process start time) from `/bin/ps` — a PID reused by another matching MCP child within the grace period has a different start time, so the SIGKILL is correctly aborted even when command and ancestry match
3. **Command class + ancestry**: re-confirms the PID is still a `SkyComputerUseClient` MCP child descendant of the original ancestor PID

The timer is `unref()`'d so it does not keep the event loop alive. The kill path is macOS-gated (`process.platform !== "darwin"` early return) — no change to the platform guard.

Collision check: searched open PRs for `killStaleComputerUseMcpChildren`, `SIGKILL`, `lstart`, `computer-use`; no same-file or same-problem open PR was found.

## User Impact

Codex app-server health monitor now reliably terminates stale Computer Use MCP child processes, even those that ignore SIGTERM. PID reuse is guarded by immutable launch identity (`lstart`) comparison — a replacement MCP child with the same command and ancestry will not be mistakenly killed.

## Evidence

Exact head: `14f57eb24a72fbb083215b6a77e34b72caa5acfd`

`oxfmt --check extensions/codex/src/app-server/computer-use.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/computer-use.test.ts` — passed.
`git diff --check` — passed; exit 0.

### Tests

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/codex/src/app-server/computer-use.test.ts

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  37 passed (37)
   Start at  16:45:12
   Duration  48.26s
```

Tests cover:
- SIGTERM is sent to identified stale MCP children
- After 2s grace period, revalidation confirms identity (PID + lstart + command + ancestry) → SIGKILL sent
- After 2s, quick existence check (`kill 0`) throws ESRCH → SIGKILL skipped
- After 2s, revalidation ps shows different command → SIGKILL skipped
- **After 2s, revalidation ps shows same command but different lstart → SIGKILL skipped (PID reuse guard)**

### Real behavior proof

A standalone proof script exercises the same process lifecycle on a real OS (Linux, Node 24):

```
Ancestor PID (this script): 1555975
Child PID: 1556026
ps revalidation: pid=1556026 ppid=1555975
    command: /usr/local/node/bin/node -e process.on('SIGTERM', ...)
    descendant of 1555975: YES (PASS)
Sent SIGTERM to child 1556026
After SIGTERM: child alive = true (expect true)         ← child traps SIGTERM
Waiting 2s grace period...
Revalidation: pid=1556026 exists, command marker: true  ← identity confirmed
Sent SIGKILL to child 1556026
After SIGKILL: child alive = false (expect false)       ← SIGKILL succeeds
ps after SIGKILL: pid 1556026 in list = false (expect false)

ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 1 passed, 0 failed
```

### Mutation checks

- Revert SIGKILL escalation → test "revalidates process identity and sends SIGKILL" FAILS: `expected "kill" to be called with arguments: [ 1234, 'SIGKILL' ]`, received only `SIGTERM`. Restore → 37/37 passed.
- Revert `lstart` identity check → test "skips SIGKILL when PID was reused by another matching MCP child" FAILS: SIGKILL is sent to the replacement process. Restore → 37/37 passed.

### Not tested

- macOS live process lifecycle (SIGTERM→SIGKILL on Darwin; the function is macOS-gated)
- Real Codex MCP child processes in a running macOS app-server
- PID reuse race condition in production (tested via unit tests with timer mocking)

target.title: fix(ui): bound chat avatar metadata and image fetches
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`refreshChatAvatar` in `ui/src/pages/chat/chat-avatar.ts` issues two `fetch` calls — the avatar metadata lookup and the local avatar image download — **without any timeout or abort signal**. A stalled gateway leaves avatar resolution pending indefinitely, blocking the chat header update.

This is the same unbounded-network-operation class fixed across many `fix(...)` "bound X" PRs: a request with no `AbortSignal` can hang the caller forever.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add an `AbortController` + `setTimeout` watchdog (`CHAT_AVATAR_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000`) around both fetches, matching the Control UI convention used by `agent-select.ts` (`AGENT_SELECT_AVATAR_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS`). The timer is cleared in `finally`.

## User Impact

Avatar loading fails fast instead of hanging when the gateway is slow or unreachable.

## Evidence

- `ui/src/pages/chat/chat-avatar.ts` on `main`: both `fetch` calls have no `signal`.
- Fix threads `controller.signal` into both requests and clears the timeout.

Co-Authored-By: opencode <noreply@opencode.ai>
## Real behavior proof

Behavior or issue addressed: Chat avatar resolution (`refreshChatAvatar` in `ui/src/pages/chat/chat-avatar.ts`) hangs the chat header forever when the gateway/relay avatar-metadata endpoint never responds, because both the metadata fetch and the local image fetch have no abort signal.

Real environment tested: macOS 15, Node v24.18.0 (Homebrew node@24), vitest 4.1.9, local HTTP server (`node:http`) bound to 127.0.0.1:0. Real `fetch` is used against that server; only relative-URL resolution is bridged to the local origin. To keep Node's native `fetch` scheduling working, the normal-case test runs under real timers while the stalled-case test uses fake timers to fire the 30s watchdog without waiting in real time.

Exact steps or command run after this patch:
- `npx vitest run ui/src/pages/chat/chat-avatar.test.ts`

Evidence after fix:
```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
 - aborts a stalled metadata fetch after the bound instead of hanging (pass)
 - still resolves a normal metadata + image round trip             (pass)
```

Observed result after fix: With the metadata endpoint accepting the connection but never ending the response, `refreshChatAvatar` returns via its abort/catch path after the 30s bound instead of remaining pending. With the endpoint returning 200 JSON plus a local image URL that also returns 200, `refreshChatAvatar` completes and sets the host avatar URL. Ordinary avatar loading is unaffected.

What was not tested: A full live Control UI browser session against a real gateway was not executed (no gateway credentials / headless browser in this environment). The proof exercises the exact production fetch/timeout/abort code path against a real local server, which is the behavior the change governs; the browser-only difference is relative-URL resolution, which is bridged in the test.

target.title: fix(config): ignore inherited keys when restoring env refs
target.body:
## Summary

Use `Object.hasOwn(parsed, key)` when restoring environment references so inherited properties are not treated as authored configuration.

## What Problem This Solves

`restoreEnvVarRefs` accepts plain-object values whose prototype may be customized. Its object branch iterates own `incoming` entries, but the previous `key in parsed` check also admitted inherited `parsed` properties. An inherited environment-reference template could therefore replace an incoming own value even though that template was never authored on the parsed object.

## Root Cause

- `in` traverses the prototype chain.
- `Object.hasOwn` matches the authored-key semantics used by adjacent config helpers.
- `isPlainObject` intentionally accepts custom prototypes, so narrowing the membership check is the correct local owner-boundary fix.

## Why This Fix

- One canonical own-property check at the restoration decision.
- No parser normalization, compatibility shim, or broader `isPlainObject` contract change.
- Matches sibling config-path and merge-patch own-key handling.

## User Impact

Normal JSON and JSON5 config behavior is unchanged. Internal or custom callers that pass plain objects with custom prototypes no longer restore inherited environment-reference templates.

## Evidence

- The original submitted test also passed with the old implementation, so the maintainer fixup replaced it.
- The repaired regression creates a custom prototype carrying an inherited template.
- With `key in parsed`, the focused suite fails because the inherited template is restored.
- With `Object.hasOwn`, the incoming value is preserved.

## Tests and Validation

- Blacksmith Testbox baseline: 1 focused regression failure with the old membership check.
- Blacksmith Testbox fixed: `src/config/env-preserve.test.ts` passed, 72/72 tests.
- Targeted `oxfmt --check` passed.
- Maintainer autoreview passed with no findings.
- Exact-head hosted CI is required before merge.

## Changelog

Not required: internal hardening with no documented JSON or JSON5 behavior change.

target.title: refactor(macos): move PortGuardian state to SQLite
target.body:
Stacked on #110392. Review and merge after that PR.

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where the macOS PortGuardian orphan-tunnel ledger remains in a host-global JSON file even though OpenClaw already ships a canonical SQLite table for the same durable records. JSON read/merge/write coordination can lose tunnel ownership during crashes or concurrent app activity, leaving SSH children occupying local ports without a reliable recovery receipt.

## Why This Change Was Made

PortGuardian now uses the existing `macos_port_guardian_records` table in the host-global OpenClaw state database. The logical record shape remains unchanged: `pid`, `port`, `command`, `mode`, and `timestamp`. This is additive at the schema and API boundaries: no table change, schema-version bump, wire-format change, or dual-write path.

The shared Apple SQLite bootstrap/validation code moves into `OpenClawNativeState`, so device identity and PortGuardian compose the same exact canonical version-zero tables before Node expands the database to the full schema.

Legacy `port-guard.json` is a one-time migration input only. Migration snapshots under the shipped Darwin lock, plans process reconciliation outside both the file lock and SQLite transaction, revalidates the exact source, applies a short synchronous transaction, verifies receipts, and retires the JSON file. Runtime then reads and writes SQLite only.

This migration deliberately lives in native runtime, unlike ordinary Doctor-owned state migration. Older shipped macOS writers coordinate through the Darwin file lock and can appear while the app is running. Only the native owner can participate in that lock, apply the Security.framework/CDHash mixed-copy gate, finish asynchronous process inspection before the transaction, then reacquire and revalidate the authoritative source for a short synchronous SQLite commit. Node Doctor cannot safely provide those native coordination or code-signing guarantees.

Mixed-version app copies fail closed. A signed storage-capability marker is accepted only when Security.framework metadata matches the running process kernel CDHash. Tunnel launch holds a guardian reservation from completed legacy reconciliation through process spawn and durable receipt commit; no concurrent store open or migration can enter that unrecorded window.

## User Impact

macOS SSH tunnel ownership and orphan cleanup become transactionally durable across concurrent app instances, PID reuse, crashes, delayed teardown, and legacy migration. Fresh installs no longer create the JSON ledger or lock sidecar.

This is a one-way storage cutover. Downgrading afterward to an older JSON-only app does not expose receipts written only to SQLite; rollback requires restoring a compatible backup or upgrading again.

## Maintainer Decision

Approve both deliberate contracts before merge:

1. The native-runtime migration exception above, bounded to interoperability with the shipped Darwin lock and signed mixed-copy detection.
2. The one-way downgrade/mixed-version contract: old JSON-only copies must not share the migrated state directory.

## Evidence

- Exact rebased head: `0fa751207e10debaba47e22e6840e09d9cf499db`; clean stacked merge onto #110392.
- Developer-ID-signed candidate embedded that exact head and storage marker `2`; released v2026.7.1 was independently signature-valid and had no marker.
- Disposable macOS VM, real signed apps: mixed-version exclusion preserved the legacy ledger and live SSH child without opening the SQLite table; one-time migration retired JSON and preserved one exact receipt; a second launch left it unchanged; SQLite orphan recovery killed the orphan and compare-deleted its receipt.
- Signed-app terminal proof ended `SIGNED_PORTGUARDIAN_PROOF=PASS`. Unified logs showed the legacy-copy gate and `reaped orphaned ssh tunnel (pid 3680, local port 43123)`.
- 47 focused Swift tests passed across `PortGuardianRecordStoreTests`, `LowCoverageHelperTests`, and `RemotePortTunnelTests`, including concurrency, rollback, schema validation, migration races, spawn reservation, PID reuse, and a real orphan process.
- Remote exact-head proof: 87 Node state-database tests and 489 database-first guard tests passed; full changed-surface type, lint, format, boundary, docs, and package gates passed.
- Fresh branch autoreview reported no accepted/actionable findings; patch correct confidence 0.84.
- VM proof was guest-only. The original snapshot was restored and the VM stopped; no host runtime state was touched.

AI assistance was used for implementation and review. Maintainer-directed design, focused tests, exact-head remote validation, and signed native behavior proof were performed before handoff.

The existing shared `open-path` helper is now the canonical owner of the platform launcher lifecycle. macOS `open` and Windows PowerShell waits have a five-second deadline. Linux `xdg-open` is detached and observed for immediate startup failures for five seconds; bounded startup stderr is preserved for actionable headless-environment diagnostics, then the pipe remains drained so a foreground application can keep running without receiving `SIGPIPE` or accumulating output in the Gateway.

Both `sessions.files.reveal` and `config.openFile` remain thin callers. They retain their own validation, logging, and user-facing error wording while sharing timeout, detach, stderr-draining, and failure-propagation behavior. This also provides the canonical lifecycle requested by the review of this PR and avoids duplicating it with https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109126.

Missing or immediately failing launchers still produce an actionable RPC-specific error, including bounded `xdg-open` startup diagnostics, while Linux foreground applications can remain open after the request completes.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`getClaimingHookTimeoutMs` in `src/plugins/hooks.ts:499-504` is a copy-paste of `getModifyingHookTimeoutMs` but incorrectly kept the `modifyingHookTimeoutMsByHook` dictionary as its fallback. Since no claiming-specific timeout dictionary exists, claiming hooks silently inherit timeouts intended for modifying hooks. A claiming hook using `before_agent_reply` would inherit the 3000ms modifying timeout instead of having no timeout.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix removes the erroneous fallback to `modifyingHookTimeoutMsByHook`. Only `hook.timeoutMs` (the per-registration timeout) is used for claiming hooks.

## User Impact

- Before: Claiming hooks could inherit timeouts from modifyingHookTimeoutMsByHook entries (e.g. before_agent_reply=3000ms)
- After: Claiming hooks only use their own hook.timeoutMs if explicitly set
- Modifying hooks are completely unaffected

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** getClaimingHookTimeoutMs uses modifyingHookTimeoutMsByHook as fallback, causing claiming hooks to inherit modifying timeouts
- **Real environment tested:** Linux x86_64, Node 24, commit `0da592392` on branch `fix/claiming-hook-timeout-dictionary` (rebased on upstream/main `94e1cc9a4`)
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** `node --import tsx /tmp/verify-hook-runner-invoke.mjs` — real OpenClaw `createHookRunner` runtime invocation: creates a mock registry with a `before_agent_reply` claiming hook that delays 500ms (no explicit timeoutMs), then calls `runner.runBeforeAgentReply()` with `modifyingHookTimeoutMsByHook.before_agent_reply=50ms`. On buggy code the claiming hook would inherit the 50ms modifying timeout and abort early; on fixed code the hook runs to completion (~500ms).
- **Evidence after fix:** Terminal capture of `node` runtime verification (copied live output):

  ```text
  Real OpenClaw createHookRunner runtime test for Bug 3:

  Test scenario: claiming hook (before_agent_reply) delays 500ms
  modifyingHookTimeoutMsByHook.before_agent_reply = 50ms (would affect claiming on buggy code)

  Result: undefined
  Elapsed: 501ms

  [PASS] Claiming hook completed (~500ms) - no incorrect modifying timeout applied

  Verdict: PASS (real createHookRunner invocation, hook ran to completion)
  ```

- **Observed result after fix:** Claiming hook completed in 501ms (full 500ms delay), proving no incorrect modifying timeout was inherited. On buggy code, the hook would have timed out at ~50ms.
- **What was not tested:** Other claiming hook entry points (inbound_claim); same fix applies symmetrically

target.title: fix(plugins): bound plugin manifest metadata file reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Plugin manifest metadata scan reads `openclaw.plugin.json` files from installed, bundled, and global plugin directories through unbounded `fs.readFileSync`. A corrupted or hostile manifest file could therefore exhaust memory during metadata enumeration.

## Why This Change Was Made

Plugin manifest files are small metadata descriptors like workspace hook manifests. The shared bounded `readRegularFileSync` helper with the same 256 KiB maximum used by the full plugin manifest loader now enforces the cap during metadata scanning as well. An oversized manifest is logged and skipped; scanning continues for remaining plugins.

## User Impact

Oversized plugin manifests are warned about and skipped. Metadata scan continues for other plugins.

## Maintainer Changes

- Added `PLUGIN_MANIFEST_METADATA_MAX_BYTES = 256 * 1024` constant, matching the existing limit in the full plugin manifest loader (`src/plugins/manifest.ts` `MAX_PLUGIN_MANIFEST_BYTES`).
- Replaced unbounded `fs.readFileSync` with `readRegularFileSync` bounded reader.
- Handles oversized files via `readRegularFileSync` error (plain `Error` with "exceeds" message): logs a subsystem warning and returns `undefined` so the oversized plugin is skipped.
- Added two bounding coverage tests: oversized manifest skipped, exact-limit manifest accepted.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof: bounded manifest read via listOpenClawPluginManifestMetadata

The bounded reader correctly handles all three cases — normal, oversized, and exact-limit manifests — against the **real** discovered plugin tree including source checkout, bundled, and global plugin paths. The run uses a fresh OPENCLAW_HOME with no SQLite state DB, so `readPersistedInstalledPluginIndexSync` returns null (bypasses the SQLite WAL-safety check entirely).

**Subsystem warning output (stderr):**

```
[WARN] [plugins/manifest-metadata-scan] Ignoring oversized plugin manifest at /tmp/.../big-plugin/openclaw.plugin.json: file exceeds the 262144-byte limit
```

**Scan results:**

```
── Test data ──
Good manifest size:    51 bytes
Oversized manifest:    262145 bytes (> 256 KiB)
Exact manifest size:   262144 bytes (== 256 KiB)

── Scan results ──
Total plugins discovered:  150
good-plugin found:          true
big-plugin (oversized):     false (expected: false — skipped)
exact-plugin (256 KiB):     true (expected: true — accepted)

── Verification ──
  ✅ Oversized manifest skipped
  ✅ Valid plugin still discovered
  ✅ Exact-limit manifest accepted

ALL CHECKS PASSED
```

The 150 discovered plugins include all bundled extensions and the test good-plugin, confirming that manifest discovery continues normally after the oversized entry is skipped.

target.title: fix(gateway): bound usage.list days parameter to 100 years
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`parseDays` in `src/gateway/server-methods/usage.ts` accepted any finite number, including `1e300`. Downstream `resolveTrailingDays` feeds this into `Date.UTC(year, month, day + (-1e300))`, which overflows the ECMAScript Date range and produces `NaN`. The caller then surfaces a misleading `"calendar day does not exist in requested time zone"` error instead of indicating the real problem: the `days` parameter is absurdly large.

```js
// Current behavior: 1e300 is finite, so parseDays returns 1e300
parseDays(1e300) // -> 1e300
// resolveTrailingDays then does:
Date.UTC(year, month, day - 1e300) // -> NaN
// Final user-visible error: "calendar day does not exist in requested time zone"
```

## Fix

Introduce `MAX_USAGE_DAYS = 366 * 100` (100 years, 36600 days). `parseDays` now returns `undefined` for day counts above this bound, which causes `resolveDateRange` to fall back to the default 30-day trailing window. Callers wanting truly unbounded history should use `range: "all"`.

## Evidence

New regression test covers the overflow case:

```
src/gateway/server-methods/usage.test.ts
  ✓ parseDays rejects absurd day counts that would overflow Date arithmetic
```

Test asserts:
- `parseDays(1e300)` → `undefined`
- `parseDays("1e300")` → `undefined`
- `parseDays(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER)` → `undefined`
- `parseDays(366 * 100)` → `36600` (100-year bound still accepted)

Full test run for `usage.test.ts`:

```
Test Files  2 passed (2)
Tests  82 passed (82)
Duration  90.81s
```

Existing `parseDays coerces strings/numbers to integers` test continues to pass, confirming normal inputs (7.9 → 7, "30" → 30) are unaffected.

target.title: fix(plugins): clean stale install target after double-fault persistence rollback
target.body:
## Summary

When a plugin install fails AFTER writing the install record to SQLite but BEFORE committing config, and the SQLite rollback also fails, the cleanup path misidentifies the surviving record as a prior committed install and skips target directory removal, permanently blocking retries.

- Problem: `cleanupFailedManagedPluginInstall` reads post-failure install records from SQLite and treats any record that owns the target directory as evidence of a prior committed install. In a double-fault scenario (config write fails → SQLite rollback also fails), the surviving record is actually stale data from the current failed transaction.
- Solution: Take a pre-persist snapshot of install records before the persistence attempt, pass it to the cleanup helper, and use it to distinguish a stale left-over from a genuinely previously committed install.
- What changed: `src/plugins/management-service.ts` (+35 lines — `persistManagedPluginInstall` loads pre-persist snapshot and passes it; `cleanupFailedManagedPluginInstall` accepts `previousInstallRecords` param and removes stale targets when the record wasn't present before the failed install)
